doc.title: Hubert Laws — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
title: The NEA downplaying his classical background
summary: Brown asks why the Jazz Masters presentation downplayed Laws's classical training. Laws says he had not thought about it, and they agree he bridged both worlds.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Being honored: NEA Jazz Masters and other awards

blocks.x: You’re talking about – again, I think anybody who followed your career knows that the concert music tradition has figured very prominently into your sound, your conception, your musicality, across the board. It was – what was surprising when we went to the NEA Jazz Masters, they kind of downplayed that. They talked about your gospel background and your familiarity with vernacular black music and jazz. But they downplayed that. Maybe did they feel that was too obvious? Or was that even something that you took note of?
I didn’t. You said they downplayed the fact that . . .
. . . that you had this classical training, this classical background. I don’t recall . . .
You’re right. They did not mention that too much.
Right.
Maybe because it’s the Jazz Masters.
But this is a Jazz Masters interview. We’re going to have to talk about – this is about you. I mean, this is you. You can’t deny it.
Yeah, but isn’t it in the brochure that was . . . ?

Oh, it’s in the book, but it just caught me by surprise that here you, among the pioneers of being able to bridge those two worlds, and I would have valorized that, that you were able to have that facility and the success in both fields. To me, that’s something you would want to extol, rather than to downplay.
Hmm. Interesting. I didn’t think about it too much.
Okay.

Maybe it should have been. Because, here again, the music’s more important than me. That’s the way I think about it. I’m just a participant, but the music’s more important. Maybe it would have been to the advantage to show that the classical and jazz and Latin and all that stuff can contribute to the whole of the jazz performance. In that way it could have helped. That way any aspiring musicians can also involve themselves in different idioms.

For me, like you say, I believe music is a healing force. I saw a picture in your photo gallery over there of you and Wynton very close. Wynton got all the accolades for being able to bridge both worlds, but you – for me, you pioneered that. Like I said, this was the soundtrack to my college years. I was studying music formally. Here I heard, oh,
a jazz musician playing classical and being able to straddle both and do both at such an exceptional, phenomenal level. So that was . . .
I see. I see what you mean. It could have been. But I didn’t think about it much.
Okay, well, again, not just so much that, but to me, this is really inextricable from who you are. This is who you are. You’re the – for me, you’re the one who showed that you can excel in both.
Guess what? As I come to think of it, when we played our intro to Stella, it had a classical sound.
It was all classical.
It was just totally ethereal.
Right. And that’s what I love, because you showed that we could be in a jazz context, but we can speak any language.
There you go. So there it was.
